evidence.source: CUHK Humanum, 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.field: 形義通解 / glyph forms / dated uses
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 好 as 女 plus 子 and favors a mother–child affection interpretation because early 子 forms are child-shaped and smaller than 女. It records competing proposals: a beautiful woman (Duan Yucai) and affection between a man and woman (Xu Kai and Chen Weizhan). The entry says early written uses employ extended meanings and do not attest the proposed mother–child affection sense directly. It dates the surname use 婦好 to Shang oracle-bone and bronze material, cites oracle-bone 《合集》154, 婦好娩, and identifies Fu Hao as a Shang military leader. It reports that bronze inscriptions first show the sense ‘good/beautiful’ (虘鐘: 用樂好賓), also ‘friendly’ (杜伯盨: 好朋友), and a phonetic loan for 孝 on 羌伯簋. Warring States bamboo texts attest ‘like’ (郭店《老子甲》32) and ‘friendly/peace’ (清華簡《繫年》39, 108). Some Warring States bamboo forms use 丑 in place of 女. The page lists one oracle-bone form and 13 of 129 bronze forms; the glyph images were not visually inspected here.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 好

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry reports that early oracle-bone and bronze component placement was not fixed: 女 and 子 could appear on either side, without changing the character. It cites a Han-mirror inscription variant and later forms, and treats the side-switched graph as a variant rather than a chronological ancestor. It also records the Shuowen analysis and variants where the graph is written with 女 and 丑; this modern editorial account does not establish a direct ancestry among all listed forms.
evidence.title: [A00883] 好 — 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: ShuoWen.org, digitized 說文解字 and 段玉裁注
evidence.text: The transmitted Shuowen entry defines 好 as 美 and analyzes it as 从女、子; it gives the fanqie 呼皓切. Xu Kai’s later note says 子 can praise a man and classifies the graph as associative. Duan Yucai’s Qing annotation reads 好 as originally referring to a woman and extended to beauty generally, while retaining the woman-plus-child analysis. These are historical lexicographic interpretations, not direct proof of the graph’s original motivation or earliest use.
evidence.title: 說文解字「好」

evidence.text: The entry presents the familiar 女 + 子 associative analysis and records competing explanations, including maternal affection, beauty, a man–woman relationship, and a girl’s demeanor. It characterizes the good and like readings as related by Old Chinese *-s suffixation. Its Baxter–Sagart data gives Mandarin hǎo ‘good’: Middle Chinese xawX, Old Chinese *qʰˤuʔ; hào ‘love, like (verb)’: xawH, *qʰˤuʔ-s. This is a proposed historical morphology, not evidence that the two senses arose in the order presented by a gloss list. The entry compares a limited set of Sino-Tibetan forms for ‘raise/rear/nourish’, notes a possible relationship with 畜, mentions Tibetan mkho ‘necessary, important’, and says Central Bai hux ‘good’ may be borrowed from Chinese; these comparisons are tentative and do not establish a secure external etymology. It shows Shang, Western Zhou, seal-script, and later glyph categories, but I did not inspect the glyph images.
evidence.title: 好 — Wiktionary

evidence.text: The module explicitly identifies its reconstructions as Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese and lists hǎo ‘good’ as xawX, *qʰˤuʔ, and hào ‘love, like (verb)’ as xawH, *qʰˤuʔ-s. These are reconstructed readings of 好 in two lexical uses, not pronunciation evidence for 女 or 子 as components; neither component functions as a proposed phonetic element in the dossier’s analysis.
evidence.title: Module:zh/data/och-pron-BS/好 — Wiktionary

evidence.text: The entry lists Standard Mandarin hǎo in Hanyu Pinyin and Guangzhou–Hong Kong Cantonese hou2 in Jyutping for the ‘good’ reading. The character has no proposed phonetic component here, so no component-to-character sound correspondence is being claimed.

evidence.text: The page quotes Shuowen 呼皓切 and records Guangyun entries 呼晧 and 呼到, with the first associated with upper tone and the second with departing tone in the listed Middle Chinese categories. Its system does not provide a modern IPA pronunciation; the two fanqie readings support distinct historical reading categories, not an independent account of semantic chronology.

gaps: The early graph is analyzed as 女 plus 子, but the earliest attested semantic value is uncertain: CUHK identifies Shang 婦好 as a surname and says the underlying surname graph may be a homograph written 女 + 子 with 子 phonetic and read as 子. The pronunciation/readings and the lexical graph should not be collapsed without further evidence.

The mother–child affection, woman’s beauty, and man–woman affection accounts are source-attributed hypotheses. The source’s small 子 and component scale support its preference for the mother–child account, but early inscriptional examples cited there do not directly attest that proposed sense.

The record gives selected Shang, Western Zhou, Warring States, and transmitted lexicographic examples, but not a securely dated earliest use for ordinary 好 ‘good’ or a complete dated sequence for its extensions. No chronology is inferred from the modern gloss list.

Graphic change is only partly described in the inspected prose: early 女/子 placement can vary, some Warring States bamboo forms replace 女 with 丑, and later standard form is associated with seal script. Specific inscription images were not visually inspected, and I cannot independently verify the physical glyph sequences or dating of every cited vessel.

The two readings are reconstructed in Baxter–Sagart as *qʰˤuʔ and *qʰˤuʔ-s and have distinct Guangyun fanqie/tone categories; the suffixal relationship is a linguistic analysis, not direct evidence for which semantic sense is oldest. A primary source for the Zhengzhang forms in the dossier was not successfully inspected.

No component is proposed as phonetic in the ordinary 好 analysis, so a phonetic-series component comparison was not required. The surname homograph analysis is distinct: CUHK attributes to Tang Lan and Zhang Zhenglang the proposal that 子 supplies sound and that this 好 is read 子; the early period object of discussion is the graph in a personal name, not an otherwise demonstrated phonetic role for 子 in every 好 graph.

Potential Sino-Tibetan cognacy and Central Bai borrowing are tentative source comparisons. The inspected material does not independently establish sound correspondences, borrowing direction, or dated donor and recipient attestations.

The Taiwan variants page cites sources for graphic variants, but several referenced paleographic works are not openly viewable there; the distinction between positional variants and chronological ancestry is therefore only supported to the level stated in that page.
